message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | Key Points | |------|------------------------|------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Must be returned within 30 days after you move out (unless you give a written notice of intent to stay).
• Landlord may keep up to one month’s rent for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Landlord must provide an itemized list of deductions.
• If you dispute, you can file a claim in small‑claims court. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity). | • Texas Property Code §92.001 requires “reasonable repairs” within a reasonable time. | | **Lease Terms** | • Written lease must include:
- Rent amount and due date
- Security deposit amount
- Lease term
- Rules for pets, smoking, subletting, etc. | • Oral leases are enforceable but harder to prove. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but increases must be in writing and given at least 30 days’ notice for month‑to‑month tenants. | • For fixed‑term leases, rent can only change at the start of a new term unless both parties agree. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a written notice:
- 3‑day notice to pay rent or vacate (for nonpayment)
- 30‑day notice to vacate (for lease violations)
- 60‑day notice to vacate (for ending a month‑to‑month tenancy) | • After notice, landlord files a complaint in district court.
• Tenants can contest in court; they have the right to a hearing. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Landlord cannot enter without proper notice (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, age, source of income, etc. | • Fair Housing Act applies to all residential rentals. | | **Pet Policies** | • Landlord may require a pet deposit or fee, but cannot discriminate against tenants with disabilities who use service animals. | • Texas law allows landlords to charge a pet fee, but it must be reasonable. | | **Maintenance Requests** | • Tenants can request repairs in writing.
• Landlord must respond promptly. | • If repairs are not made, tenants may withhold rent or repair and deduct (though this is risky and should be done carefully). | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Tenants may sublet or assign the lease only with landlord’s written consent (unless the lease says otherwise). | • Landlord can’t unreasonably deny consent. | | **Right to Access Records** | • Tenants can request copies of lease agreements, security deposit receipts, and maintenance logs. | • Landlord must provide within a reasonable time. | | **Legal Remedies** | • Small‑claims court (up to $20,000) for disputes over deposits, unpaid rent, or damages.
• Civil court for eviction disputes. | • Tenants can also file complaints with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local housing agencies. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Get a Written Lease** – Read it thoroughly; ask questions about any ambiguous clauses. 2. **Document the Condition** – Take photos or videos of the unit before you move in; keep a copy of the move‑in inspection report. 3. **Know Your Deposit** – Verify the amount and the conditions under which it can be withheld. 4. **Understand Notice Requirements** – Know how much notice you need to give if you plan to leave early. 5. **Keep Records** – Save all communications with your landlord (emails, texts, letters). --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Property Code** | Statutory rights and obligations | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, fair‑housing enforcement | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/ | | **Local Housing Courts** | Eviction filings, small‑claims disputes | Search your county court website | | **Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal advice | e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar association referral services | | **Tenant Rights Guides** | Summaries of rights, checklists | e.g., Texas Tenants’ Guide by the Texas A&M Law Review | --- #### Common Misconceptions | Myth | Reality | |------|---------| | *“I can just stop paying rent if the landlord doesn’t fix things.”* | Withholding rent can lead to eviction and legal action. It’s safer to file a formal complaint or seek court relief. | | *“Landlords can charge unlimited fees for pets.”* | Fees must be reasonable and disclosed in the lease. | | *“If I sign a lease, I’m locked in forever.”* | Most leases are for a fixed term; after that, you can negotiate renewal or termination with proper notice. | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have clear statutory protections regarding security deposits, habitability, notice requirements, and discrimination. Knowing these rights—and having a written lease that reflects them—helps you avoid disputes and gives you a solid foundation if you ever need to take legal action. If you encounter a problem, start by documenting everything, communicate in writing, and consider seeking help from a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid organization.
